name: Side-Channel & Microarchitectural Attacks
description: Timing, cache, power, EM, and speculative-execution (Spectre/Meltdown) side channels and defenses.

ccs.narrative:
Research on side channels at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on side-channel attacks, timing leaks, and covert channels. Parallel contributions—Fallout: Leaking Data on Meltdown-resistant CPUs (2019) and ret2spec: Speculative Execution Using Return Stack Buffers (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. DNS Cache Poisoning Attack Reloaded: Revolutions with Side Channels (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating Revives DNS cache poisoning by exploiting side channels in the network stack to defeat randomization-based defenses. Other strong contributions included One Glitch to Rule Them All: Fault Injection Attacks Against AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (2021), Prime+Scope: Overcoming the Observer Effect for High-Precision Cache Contention Attacks (2021), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. Password-Stealing without Hacking: Wi-Fi Enabled Practical Keystroke Eavesdropping (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Eavesdrops keystrokes via commodity Wi-Fi signals without hacking hardware, stealing passwords. Similarly, Recovering Fingerprints from In-Display Fingerprint Sensors via Electromagnetic Side Channel (2023) and Exploration of Power Side-Channel Vulnerabilities in Quantum Computer Controllers (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

ndss.narrative:
Side-channel and microarchitectural attack research at NDSS has expanded from CPU cache timing to an eclectic set of physical emanation channels. ZeroTrace (NDSS 2018) proposed Intel SGX-based oblivious RAM as a software countermeasure against memory-access-pattern leakage, one of the first practical defenses against hardware side channels in cloud settings. Privacy Attacks to the 4G and 5G Cellular Paging Protocols Using Side Channels (NDSS 2019) then demonstrated that cellular protocol timing leaks enable subscriber tracking, a threat model distinct from classical cache attacks.

The 2020–2022 period introduced acoustic, power, and vibration channels. Learning-based Practical Smartphone Eavesdropping with Built-in Accelerometers (NDSS 2020) reconstructed speech from motion-sensor data; GhostTalk (NDSS 2022) eavesdropped on voice commands via power-line measurements; and Hunting the Haunter (NDSS 2021) applied symbolic execution to detect Spectre gadgets at scale, keeping the microarchitectural thread alive.

The 2023–2025 cohort has pushed into more exotic domains. Copy-on-Flip (NDSS 2023) addressed Rowhammer as a side-channel enabler for persistent bit flips in ECC memory; Eavesdropping on Controller Acoustic Emanation for Keystroke Inference in VR (NDSS 2024) showed that VR handheld controllers leak keystrokes acoustically; and I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025) revealed a KV-cache side channel in shared LLM inference infrastructure—evidence that side channels follow computational resources wherever they migrate.

uss.narrative:
The earliest works in this list mark the watershed moment for microarchitectural security: the disclosure of transient-execution attacks. "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) showed that out-of-order execution lets an unprivileged process read protected kernel memory, shattering the assumption that hardware-enforced memory isolation was a hard boundary. The same year, "Foreshadow: Extracting the Keys to the Intel SGX Kingdom with Transient Out-of-Order Execution" (USENIX 2018) carried the idea into trusted execution environments, dumping SGX enclave secrets and sealing keys. Around them, a wave of more classical side-channel work matured: cache-protection bypasses via the TLB in "Translation Leak-aside Buffer" (USENIX 2018), the EM-based single-trace RSA recovery of "One&Done" (USENIX 2018), and the off-path Wi-Fi timing channel of "Off-Path TCP Exploit" (USENIX 2018) — together signaling that leakage could come from caches, TLBs, EM emanations, and network timing alike.

The following years shifted from discovery to systematization and defense, and from CPU caches to the whole microarchitecture. Defensive proposals like "ScatterCache: Thwarting Cache Attacks via Cache Set Randomization" (USENIX 2019) and the speculation-hardening of "DOLMA" (USENIX 2021) and "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) tried to close the channels, while attackers broadened the attack surface: "SPOILER" (USENIX 2019) linked speculative load hazards to Rowhammer, "Medusa" (USENIX 2020) automated MDS-style data sampling, and "Lord of the Ring(s)" (USENIX 2021) demonstrated contention on the CPU's on-chip ring interconnect — a channel beyond the cache hierarchy entirely. A recurring theme was automation and measurement of the leakage surface itself, exemplified by "Osiris: Automated Discovery of Microarchitectural Side Channels" (USENIX 2021). This period also saw the field cross into machine-learning targets, as "CSI NN" (USENIX 2019) reverse-engineered neural-network architectures over an EM side channel and "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) flipped DNN weight bits.

By the early 2020s the work turned to confidential computing, hardware mitigations, and the limits of vendor fixes. "CIPHERLEAKS" (USENIX 2021) broke constant-time crypto on AMD SEV through a ciphertext side channel, and "VoltPillager" (USENIX 2021) used hardware voltage glitching against SGX. Most strikingly, papers began defeating the very mitigations deployed after Spectre: "Branch History Injection" (USENIX 2022) and "RETBLEED: Arbitrary Speculative Code Execution with Return Instructions" (USENIX 2022) showed that hardware defenses against Spectre-v2 remained bypassable, while "ÆPIC Leak" (USENIX 2022) leaked uninitialized data architecturally rather than transiently.

The most recent listed work shows the area both diversifying and returning to fundamentals. New application domains appear, such as AR/VR keylogging from head motion in "Going through the motions" (USENIX 2023), even as core hardware threats persist — "ZenHammer: Rowhammer Attacks on AMD Zen-based Platforms" (USENIX 2024) extends Rowhammer to AMD's dominant Zen platforms. Across these venues the trajectory is clear: from a few headline transient-execution breaks, the field has grown into a mature discipline that systematically discovers channels (Osiris), broadens them beyond caches (ring interconnect, power, EM), repeatedly outpaces deployed mitigations (BHI, RETBLEED), and now contends with confidential-computing and emerging-platform threats while the underlying physics of leakage remains stubbornly hard to fully close.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from 2018, mark the moment microarchitectural side channels jumped from a specialized concern to a discipline-defining crisis. "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) showed that the CPU's own out-of-order execution could be turned against the basic memory isolation every operating system depends on, reading kernel memory from an unprivileged process. "Foreshadow" (USENIX 2018) immediately carried the same transient-execution idea into Intel SGX, extracting attestation keys from the enclave that was supposed to be the trusted anchor. Alongside these, 2018 also showed how broad the attack surface had become beyond CPU caches: "FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks" (S&P 2018) leaked secrets across cloud tenants sharing programmable hardware, "Screaming Channels" (CCS 2018) coupled digital activity into a chip's radio transmitter so secrets could be read over the air, "Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical" (CCS 2018) extended timing leaks to GPUs, and "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018) kept the DRAM fault-injection thread alive against defenses meant to stop it.

2019 turned the Meltdown shock into a research program. "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019) generalized the threat to branch prediction, showing that almost any speculating CPU could be tricked into leaking data, and a wave of papers found new microarchitectural buffers to exploit: "ZombieLoad" (CCS 2019), "RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load" (S&P 2019), and "Fallout" (CCS 2019) showed that even Meltdown-resistant chips leaked data sampled from internal load and store buffers. Researchers also widened the gadget vocabulary beyond branch poisoning, with "SMoTherSpectre" and "Port Contention for Fun and Profit" (both 2019) leaking through execution-port contention. Crucially, this year also produced the first serious defensive and foundational science: "ScatterCache" (USENIX 2019) randomized cache sets to thwart eviction-based attacks, "Theory and Practice of Finding Eviction Sets" (S&P 2019) put the core attack primitive on rigorous footing, and "SoK: ...Hardware Performance Counters for Security" (S&P 2019) audited the tools defenders were relying on.

By 2020-2021 the field both deepened its attacks and matured its defenses. New leakage vectors moved into power and voltage: "Plundervolt" (S&P 2020) used software-controlled voltage scaling to inject faults into SGX, and "PLATYPUS" (S&P 2021) turned Intel's own energy-reporting interface into a software power side channel. The Rowhammer line advanced past vendor mitigations with "TRRespass" (S&P 2020) and turned read-only with "RAMBleed" (S&P 2020), while "LVI" (S&P 2020) inverted Spectre by injecting attacker values into a victim's transient execution. Defense and analysis also became principled: "Spectector" (S&P 2020) offered formal detection of speculative information flows, and "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2020) tackled network-level traffic-analysis leaks. The most recent papers show the area converging with machine-learning security, as side channels become a tool for stealing and corrupting neural networks: "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) flipped DRAM bits to degrade DNN accuracy, and "DeepSteal" (S&P 2022) leveraged the same memory leakage to steal model weights, signaling where the field now sits: a broad, cross-layer arms race spanning CPUs, accelerators, DRAM, power interfaces, and the ML models running on top of them.
